name: Pulling coconut oil for gums

card.summary: Swishing coconut oil as a gum remedy; ADA says no reliable studies support it, though the Canadian Dental Association does not expect harm.
card.note: Evidence consists of small, underpowered studies.

quick.overview:
Oil pulling means swishing an edible oil such as coconut oil in the mouth and spitting it out. It comes from Ayurvedic tradition and is promoted for gum and oral health.

The American Dental Association says no reliable studies support it; the Canadian Dental Association said in 2014 it was not convinced of benefits but did not think it would cause harm.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the oil pulls toxins out; no mechanism has been identified, and some commentators attribute any effect to mechanical swishing.
quick.risks: The Canadian Dental Association did not expect harm. The pages consulted do not discuss specific adverse events.

lead: Oil pulling with coconut oil is the practice of swishing a spoonful of the oil in the mouth for a period and spitting it out, like a mouthwash, with the aim of healthier gums, fresher breath and a cleaner-looking smile. It comes from Ayurvedic medicine, and sunflower, sesame, olive and herbal oils are also used.[1]

Practitioners say it improves oral health, and promoters often add that it draws out toxins; Wikipedia reports that no credible evidence supports the toxin claim.[1] The American Dental Association has said there are no reliable scientific studies supporting oil pulling for oral hygiene, while the Canadian Dental Association (2014) said it did not expect harm but was not convinced of particular benefits.[1]

A 2026 systematic review of 31 studies on traditional oral hygiene practices reported that oil pulling with sesame or coconut oil moderately reduced microbial load and improved gingival health, with results varying against chlorhexidine.[2]

chain: Swishing coconut oil in the mouth
Mechanical rinsing and possible effects on oral microbes
Less plaque and gum inflammation (reported in some trials)
angle.text: People swish coconut oil as an add-on to brushing, aiming for healthier gums and a cleaner mouth, which supports how the smile looks and smells. Research reports on plaque and gum scores rather than appearance.

infobox: No harm expected; not convinced of benefit[1]

paras: The user holds a small amount of edible oil in the mouth, moves it around, and spits it out afterwards, much as with mouthwash.[1]

King (2018) in the British Dental Journal reported finding no credible evidence of benefit.[1] A 2016 systematic review of randomized trials by Gbinigie and colleagues, described as the first on oil pulling and oral hygiene, found few, underpowered studies and urged cautious interpretation.[1] Steven Novella (2014) suggested any benefit may come from the mechanical act of swishing, and Lakshmi and colleagues (2013) noted that no mechanism has been established.[1]

The 2026 systematic review of 31 studies in Oral Health and Preventive Dentistry reported that sesame or coconut oil pulling moderately reduced microbial load and improved gingival health, with mixed comparisons against chlorhexidine.[2] A 2026 pilot triple-blinded trial of 30 people with periodontitis found that a coconut oil mouth rinse reduced plaque and bleeding on probing versus a placebo rinse after one month; it used a rinse rather than oil pulling.[2] A 2022 trial of 24 people with gingivitis used microneedling with coconut or sesame oil and reported reduced gingival index scores in the coconut oil group, without differences in plaque index.[2]

lore.intro: Oil pulling is discussed in wellness circles as a natural alternative to mouthwash for gums and breath.

claims.claim: Swishing coconut oil heals gums and pulls out toxins
claims.believers: Proponents say regular swishing improves gum health and removes toxins from the mouth.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports no credible evidence for toxin removal and no established mechanism, and the ADA says no reliable studies support oil pulling; a 2026 systematic review reported improved gingival health in some trials.[1][2]
